# Session 3 · Design: choosing the right study

## Week 3 · Saturday · online, 19:30-22:30

- Recap quiz on Session 2 (10 min)
- 3.1  Study designs in pictures (45 min)
- Whole-class exercise: Name that design (15 min)
- Break (15 min)
- 3.2  More designs: trial variants, pilots, quasi-experimental, qualitative (30 min)
- Whole-class exercise: choose the design (15 min)
- Proposal builder 3: design, setting and population (45 min), then wrap-up (5 min)

::: {.notes}
Start 19:30. Point: the design decides what you may claim at the end.

Ask: 'Who has ever collected data for a study?' Use them as examples later.

Clock: 19:30 recap, 19:40 3.1, 20:25 Name that design, 20:40 break, 20:55 3.2, 21:25 choose the design, 21:40 proposal builder 3, 22:25 wrap-up.

Timing: 1 minute.
:::

## Recap quiz: three questions on Session 2

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#6C3483"}
QUICK QUIZ · 9 min
:::

::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#6C3483"}
- Q1. Your PubMed search finds 3,000 papers. Add a concept with AND, or a synonym with OR?
- Q2. After the title and abstract, what do you read next in a paper?
- Q3. An abstract says 'a trend towards lower mortality (p = 0.42)'. What is this called?
- Then re-read your own research question (your Proposal Part 1 from Sessions 1 and 2): 3 min
:::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#6C3483"}
**OUTPUT** Answer each question in the poll (30 s each), then re-read your own question
:::

::: {.notes}
Three poll questions. No marks, just a warm-up. Show the results, then the next slide.

Timing: 9 minutes.
:::

## Recap quiz: answers

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Q1. AND]{.neu-card-title}

- AND adds a concept and narrows
- OR adds a synonym and widens
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Q2. Figures and tables]{.neu-card-title}

- They show the main results
- Read them before the text
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Q3. Spin]{.neu-card-title}

- p = 0.42: no clear difference
- 'A trend' makes it sound positive
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Honest version: 'mortality did not differ clearly between groups (p = 0.42)'.
:::

::: {.notes}
After Q3 ask for a rewrite, then compare it with the honest version at the bottom.

Timing: within the 9 minutes of the quiz.
:::

## Key words of the day

::: {.neu-intro}
The words you will use today (no need to memorise definitions)
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[The pieces]{.neu-card-title}

- Exposure: what comes first
- Outcome: what we count later
- Comparison group
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Who decides?]{.neu-card-title}

- Observational: we watch
- Experimental: we assign
- Randomised: chance assigns
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Which way in time?]{.neu-card-title}

- Cross-sectional: snapshot
- Case-control: look back
- Cohort: follow forward
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#055F56"}
[After the break]{.neu-card-title}

- Cluster and crossover trials
- Non-inferiority and pilot trials
- Time series, qualitative
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Two questions name most designs: who decided the exposure, and which way does time run?
:::

::: {.notes}
3.1 starts here (45 minutes). Read the four headings only.

Ask: 'In our fluid question, what is the exposure and what is the outcome?' Expected: restrictive fluids (vs usual care), death by day 28.

Timing: 1 minute.
:::

## One question, two designs

::: {.neu-intro}
In adults with septic shock, does a restrictive fluid strategy reduce 28-day mortality? Both papers were emailed before Session 1
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:2"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Paper 1: Boulet 2024, randomised trial]{.neu-card-title}

- 50 patients randomised, 48 analysed
- Restrictive (non-resuscitation) fluids vs usual care
- Primary outcome: fluid balance at day 5
- **The investigator assigns the strategy**
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Paper 2: Hyun 2023, cohort study]{.neu-card-title}

- Sepsis registry: 11,981 patients, 20 hospitals
- Positive vs negative fluid balance, days 1-3
- Outcome: death by day 28 (matched pairs)
- **The investigator observes what happened**
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Same question, two designs: the design decides what you may claim.
:::

::: {.notes}
Boulet assigned the strategy by chance. Hyun only observed. Boulet's primary outcome was fluid balance, not mortality.

Ask (poll): 'Which study would you trust more on whether restriction saves lives?' Expected: mixed. Neither answers it fully. Resolve it by the end of 3.1.

Timing: 2.5 minutes.
:::

## 3.1  Study designs in pictures

:::: {.neu-statement}
::: {.neu-big}
Did the investigator assign the exposure, or just watch?
:::

::: {.neu-sub}
That one question sorts almost every study design. (45 minutes)
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
For each design ask: who decided the exposure, and which way does time run? No need to memorise names.

Timing: 30 seconds.
:::

## Four families of study designs

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Descriptive]{.neu-card-title}

- Describes, no comparison
- Case report or case series
- Cross-sectional survey
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Observational]{.neu-card-title}

- Compares groups, we watch
- Case-control
- Cohort (prospective or retrospective)
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Experimental]{.neu-card-title}

- Compares groups, we assign
- Randomised controlled trial (RCT)
- Non-randomised trial
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Studies of studies]{.neu-card-title}

- Combine many studies
- Systematic review
- Meta-analysis
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Descriptive designs describe. Analytical designs (observational and experimental) compare groups.
:::

::: {.notes}
Observational does not mean bad: harm, prognosis and rare diseases often need it.

Poll: 'Which card for Paper 1? Paper 2?' Expected: Boulet experimental (RCT), Hyun observational (cohort).

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

## Exposure and outcome: the two words you need

| Example | Exposure (comes first) | Outcome (counted later) |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Paper 2: Hyun 2023, cohort | Positive fluid balance by day 3 | Death by day 28 |
| Paper 1: Boulet 2024, RCT | Restrictive fluid strategy | Fluid balance at day 5 |
| Another example: ICU infection | Parenteral (intravenous) nutrition | Candidaemia (Candida in the blood) |
| Another example: the ward | Air mattress | Pressure injury |

::: {.neu-table-caption}
Exposure: a treatment, strategy or risk factor. Outcome: death, infection, injury, a lab value. Comparison group: people without the exposure, or with usual care.
:::

::: {.notes}
Fluid balance is the outcome in Boulet but the exposure in Hyun. A treatment is an exposure too.

Ask: 'Name the exposure, outcome and comparison in our question.' Expected: restrictive fluids, death by day 28, usual care.

Timing: 3 minutes.
:::

## Descriptive designs: describe, do not compare

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:2"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Case report or case series]{.neu-card-title}

- A few unusual patients, described in detail
- No comparison group
- Raises ideas but cannot test them
- e.g. the first 24 critically ill COVID-19 patients in Seattle ICUs (2020)
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Cross-sectional study]{.neu-card-title}

- One snapshot of a whole unit, on one day
- Gives prevalence: how many have it now
- Exposure and outcome measured together
- Cannot show which came first
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Descriptive studies raise questions. They cannot answer 'does X cause Y?'
:::

::: {.notes}
Case series: Bhatraju et al., NEJM 2020, described the first 24 COVID-19 patients in Seattle ICUs: who they were, how they were ventilated, who died. It raised questions but compared nobody.

Cross-sectional: exposure and outcome measured at the same moment, so time order is unknown.

Ask: 'How could you measure, on one day, how common a positive fluid balance is in your ICU?' Expected: a point-prevalence survey.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

## Another example: a one-day point-prevalence survey

::: {.neu-intro}
A cross-sectional study you could run next week
:::

:::: {.neu-steps}
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Choose a day]{.neu-step-label}

- All inpatients on all wards, one weekday
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Examine everyone]{.neu-step-label}

- Two trained nurses, one standard form
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Record both]{.neu-step-label}

- Pressure injury (yes or no) and mattress type, at the same visit
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Count]{.neu-step-label}

- e.g. 37 of 412 patients = 9% prevalence today
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** A snapshot gives prevalence. It cannot show which came first.
:::

::: {.notes}
Hypothetical numbers. You cannot tell whether the mattress or the injury came first. For 'how common is it now?' this is the right design.

Ask: 'What could you measure in one day for the fluid question?' Expected: today's fluid balance and kidney function for every patient.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Case-control: pick people by outcome, then compare their past exposures.
:::

::: {.notes}
Trace the arrows right to left. Good for rare outcomes. Weaknesses: recall bias, choosing controls, confounding, odds ratio only.

Exposure must be measured the same way in both groups: same records, same questions, ideally by someone who does not know who is a case.

Case-control selects by outcome, a cohort by exposure.

Ask: 'Why can you not calculate the risk of candidaemia here?' Expected: we chose how many cases and controls.

Timing: 2.5 minutes.
:::

## Another example: a case-control study in the ICU

::: {.neu-intro}
Question: is parenteral nutrition a risk factor for candidaemia in the ICU?
:::

:::: {.neu-steps}
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Find cases]{.neu-step-label}

- 40 ICU patients with candidaemia, from lab records
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Find controls]{.neu-step-label}

- 80 ICU patients without it (2 per case), same units and months
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Look back]{.neu-step-label}

- Parenteral nutrition in the 14 days before?
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Compare]{.neu-step-label}

- Exposed: 24 of 40 cases vs 16 of 80 controls
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#055F56"}
[Report]{.neu-step-label}

- An odds ratio (OR), calculated in Session 4
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Cases and controls are chosen by outcome. Exposure is measured looking back.
:::

::: {.notes}
Take your time: Session 4 uses the same numbers to calculate the OR.

Why 80 controls? Cases are few and fixed, so extra controls add precision cheaply. Two to four controls per case is usual; beyond four, little is gained.

Controls must come from the population that produced the cases, not healthy volunteers.

Timing: 2.5 minutes.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Cohort: exposure first, outcome later, so time runs the right way.
:::

::: {.notes}
Arrows left to right. This is Paper 2. A retrospective cohort still goes from exposure to outcome.

Ask: 'In Hyun, who decided which patients got more fluid?' Expected: the clinicians, by how sick the patient looked. Hold this for Session 4.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

## Worked example: Paper 2 (Hyun 2023), step by step

::: {.neu-intro}
Read it as in Session 2. Question: is a positive fluid balance associated with death by day 28?
:::

:::: {.neu-steps}
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Define the cohort]{.neu-step-label}

- Adults with sepsis in 20 hospitals, ICU stay of 3 days or more
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Measure exposure]{.neu-step-label}

- Cumulative fluid balance, ICU days 1-3: positive or negative
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Follow forward]{.neu-step-label}

- Record who dies by day 28
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Compare]{.neu-step-label}

- Matched pairs. Day 2: a positive balance, about twice the death rate of a negative one
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** A cohort groups people by exposure and follows them to the outcome.
:::

::: {.notes}
Day 2 result: HR 2.13 (95% CI 1.48-3.06). In plain words: matched patients with a positive balance on day 2 died at about twice the rate of patients with a negative balance on day 2. Day 1: no clear difference.

The HR compares death rates over time, so it is close to, but not the same as, a ratio of risks. HR is taught in Session 6.

Timing: 3 minutes.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** In an RCT chance, not the clinician, decides who gets what.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is Paper 1 (Boulet 2024). R: randomisation by a central computer, 1:1.

An RCT is a cohort in which chance assigns the exposure, so groups are alike for measured and unmeasured factors.

6 deaths in each group: almost nothing about mortality. The pilot was powered for fluid balance.

Ask: 'Why not randomise everything?' Expected: ethics, rare or slow outcomes, cost.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

## Worked example: Paper 1 (Boulet 2024), step by step

::: {.neu-intro}
Question: does restricting non-resuscitation fluids reduce the day-5 fluid balance?
:::

:::: {.neu-steps}
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Eligibility]{.neu-step-label}

- Septic shock, age 18-85, vasopressor started less than 24 h ago
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Consent]{.neu-step-label}

- Patient or legal surrogate
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Randomise]{.neu-step-label}

- Central computer, 1:1, so nobody can predict
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Treat]{.neu-step-label}

- Restrictive vs usual care for 7 days
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#055F56"}
[Measure]{.neu-step-label}

- Fluid balance at day 5. Death by day 28
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** In a trial the investigator assigns the exposure by chance.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clinicians knew the group. Only patients and statisticians were blinded.

Poll: 'Which step makes this an experiment?' Expected: step 3, randomisation.

Timing: 2.5 minutes.
:::


::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** A systematic review searches and appraises. A meta-analysis pools the numbers.
:::

::: {.notes}
Illustrative forest plot: each square is one study, the line its 95% CI, the diamond the pooled result. A meta-analysis is only as good as the studies it pools.

Ask: 'Narrative vs systematic review?' Expected: a systematic review has a stated, reproducible search and selection.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

## Where the two papers sit on the evidence pyramid

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="38%"}
::: {.neu-side-notes}
### Read it with care

- SR / MA: systematic review and meta-analysis
- Higher = less prone to bias, on average
- A rule of thumb, not a law
- A good cohort can beat a poor RCT
- The best design is the one that fits the question
:::
:::
::: {.column width="62%"}

::: {.notes}

Poll: 'Which paper is higher, and is it more useful for our mortality question?' Expected: Boulet is higher, but it was not powered for mortality.

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Assigned? Random? Which way does time run? Three questions name the design.
:::

::: {.notes}
Walk the tree once with Boulet (assigned, random: RCT) and once with Hyun (not assigned, comparison, exposure first: cohort). Do not name designs from title words.

Poll: 'Fluid balance and kidney function of every patient on one day?' Expected: cross-sectional. 'Protocol from one date, before vs after?' Expected: non-randomised (quasi-experimental).

Timing: 5 minutes.
:::

## Every design trades something away

::: {.neu-intro}
Strengths and weaknesses at a glance
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Cross-sectional]{.neu-card-title}

- [+ quick and cheap]{style="color:#2E8B57"}
- [+ gives prevalence]{style="color:#2E8B57"}
- [- which came first?]{style="color:#B23B2E"}
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Case-control]{.neu-card-title}

- [+ rare outcomes]{style="color:#2E8B57"}
- [+ few patients, fast]{style="color:#2E8B57"}
- [- recall bias]{style="color:#B23B2E"}
- [- confounding]{style="color:#B23B2E"}
- [- odds ratio only]{style="color:#B23B2E"}
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Cohort]{.neu-card-title}

- [+ clear time order]{style="color:#2E8B57"}
- [+ can calculate risk]{style="color:#2E8B57"}
- [+ several outcomes of one exposure]{style="color:#2E8B57"}
- [- slow if prospective]{style="color:#B23B2E"}
- [- confounding]{style="color:#B23B2E"}
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[RCT]{.neu-card-title}

- [+ balances the unknown]{style="color:#2E8B57"}
- [+ strongest for cause]{style="color:#2E8B57"}
- [- costly, ethical limits]{style="color:#B23B2E"}
- [- selected patients]{style="color:#B23B2E"}
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** No design is perfect: choose the one whose weakness hurts your question least.
:::

::: {.notes}
Risk = the proportion who develop the outcome during follow-up, e.g. 30 of 100 dead by day 28. A cohort follows people from the start, so risk can be calculated in each group. A case-control study cannot do this.

Pick one strength and one weakness per card. The RCT balances unknown confounders but trial patients are selected (Boulet excluded patients over 85).

Why only an odds ratio in a case-control study: we choose how many cases and controls to take (here 40 and 80), so the share of people with the outcome is set by us, not by nature. Risks, and so risk ratios, cannot be calculated. The odds ratio does not depend on that choice.

Cohort: one exposure (e.g. a positive fluid balance) can be followed to several outcomes (death, kidney injury, days on the ventilator).

Confounding affects every observational design, case-control as well as cohort.

Ask: 'Which design for risk factors of a rare drug reaction?' Expected: case-control.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

## What can each design claim?

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:2"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[RCT: Paper 1, Boulet 2024 (48 patients)]{.neu-card-title}

- **[It can claim]{style="color:#2E8B57"}**
- Groups alike at the start (chance)
- A difference can be blamed on the strategy
- **[Its limits]{style="color:#B23B2E"}**
- Too small for mortality (6 vs 6 deaths)
- Clinicians knew the treatment (single-blind)
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Cohort: Paper 2, Hyun 2023 (thousands)]{.neu-card-title}

- **[It can claim]{style="color:#2E8B57"}**
- Large, real patients, 28-day mortality
- 'Associated with' (day 2: death rate about twice as high with a positive balance)
- **[Its limits]{style="color:#B23B2E"}**
- Cannot prove that fluid causes death
- Sicker patients got more fluid (confounding)
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** RCTs can say 'caused'. Cohorts should say 'associated'.
:::

::: {.notes}
Adjusting or matching reduces measured confounding only.

Ask for one honest conclusion per paper. Expected: Boulet 'did not clearly reduce day-5 fluid balance'. Hyun 'a positive balance on days 2-3 was associated with higher mortality'.

Timing: 4 minutes.
:::

## Check your understanding: caused or associated?

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#6C3483"}
QUICK QUIZ · 3 min
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#6C3483"}
- A. Paper 1, Boulet (RCT): 'The restrictive strategy did not reduce the day-5 fluid balance'
- B. Paper 2, Hyun (cohort): 'A positive fluid balance causes higher 28-day mortality'
- C. A one-day survey of ICU patients: 'A positive fluid balance today is associated with kidney injury today'
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#6C3483"}
For each sentence

- Is the wording right for the design?
- Vote in the poll: right or wrong
:::
:::
::::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#6C3483"}
**OUTPUT** One poll vote (right or wrong) for each sentence
:::

::: {.notes}
Three-question poll. Show the results, then the answers on the next slide.

Timing: 3 minutes.
:::

## Answers: caused or associated?

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[A. Right]{.neu-card-title}

- An RCT assigns by chance
- It may speak of an effect
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[B. Wrong]{.neu-card-title}

- A cohort only watches
- Say 'associated with'
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[C. Right]{.neu-card-title}

- A one-day survey only watches
- 'Associated with' fits
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** RCTs can say 'caused'. Observational designs say 'associated'.
:::

::: {.notes}
For B, ask for the honest rewrite: 'a positive fluid balance was associated with higher 28-day mortality'.

Timing: within the 3 minutes of the check. 3.1 ends here.
:::

## Exercise: Name that design

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#0D7377"}
WHOLE-CLASS TASK · 15 min
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#0D7377"}
- Six short abstracts on our fluid question (exercise sheet, Part A)
- For each one: which design is it, and which words in the abstract show it?
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
Use the tree

- Assigned and random: RCT
- Outcome first, look back: case-control
- Exposure first, follow forward: cohort
- Same moment: cross-sectional
:::
:::
::::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#0D7377"}
**OUTPUT** Work alone (6 min): for each abstract, write the design and the words that show it
:::

::: {.notes}
6 minutes: everyone works alone on all six. Then 9 minutes: go through them one by one, calling on two or three people for each (design, then the words that show it). Type the answer on screen.

Abstracts 3 and 4 are the hardest. If someone says 'old records, so case-control', ask: selected by outcome or by exposure?

Key: s3\_solutions, Part A. Announce the break at the end.
:::

![](images/figures/common/break_cup.png){width="32%"}

[Break]{style="color:#0D7377;font-size:1.6em;font-weight:700"}

[15 min]{style="color:#595959;font-size:0.9em"}
:::

Break 20:40-20:55. Put a countdown timer on screen. Restart on time.

:::: {.neu-statement}

Real projects bend the basic designs.

::: {.neu-sub}
Trial variants, non-inferiority, pilot studies, quasi-experimental designs and qualitative research. (30 minutes)

3.2 runs 30 minutes. Most hospital projects are unit-level changes, pilots or interviews.

Timing: 30 seconds.
:::


::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Choose the trial layout that fits the treatment and the unit of care.
:::

::: {.notes}
We are not going into much detail here, just introducing these designs so that students know they exist. If you want to know them in more depth, you can sign up for the Level 3 course on advanced topics.

R: randomisation. A and B: two treatments.

Crossover is only for stable chronic conditions, not septic shock. The disease moves fast and is unstable, so a patient can recover or die during the first treatment period and cannot "come back" for the second treatment. Point to the grey bar in the middle, labelled "washout". This is a rest period for the first drug to wear off before switching to the second. Without it, the effect of A would mix into the result for B. Stress that the order A→B or B→A is randomised. Randomisation is about the order, not about who gets which drug. Benefit: each person is their own control, so differences between people are removed. That is why fewer patients are usually needed.

Timing: 5.5 minutes.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Non-inferiority: the whole CI must stay below a margin fixed in advance.
:::

::: {.notes}
CI: confidence interval. Hypothetical results.

The margin is fixed in the protocol before the data. A superior, B non-inferior, C inconclusive, D inferior.

Boulet's p = 0.42 does not show restriction is as good as usual care.

The same rule applies to every analysis: write the plan first and stick to it. Session 6 shows why many unplanned tests produce false findings.

Poll: 'Who decides the margin?' Expected: clinicians and patients, with the statistician.

Timing: 5 minutes.
:::

## Pilot and feasibility studies: the rehearsal

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:2"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Paper 1, Boulet 2024: a pilot trial]{.neu-card-title}

- 1,201 patients screened
- 50 randomised (4%)
- 48 analysed (96%)
- About 3 patients per month across 3 ICUs
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[A pilot asks: can we do the big trial?]{.neu-card-title}

- Can we recruit enough patients?
- Will patients or families consent?
- Can staff deliver the intervention?
- Are outcomes measurable and complete?
- What numbers do we need for the big trial?
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** A pilot asks 'can we do it?', not 'does it work?'
:::

::: {.notes}
Boulet: 1,201 screened, 50 randomised, about 3 patients per month. A pilot tests feasibility, not effectiveness, and is planned as a pilot from the start.

Poll: 'Would you launch a 1,000-patient trial in the same 3 ICUs?' Expected: not as designed. It would take decades.

Timing: 4 minutes.
:::

change</div></div></div>

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Quasi-experimental: a change made without randomisation. Compare with the trend, not one 'before' average.
:::

::: {.notes}
Quasi-experimental: an intervention is introduced, but not by chance, e.g. a whole hospital starts a bundle on one date.

Before-after (left) compares one average before with one after. It is weak: rates often fall anyway.

Interrupted time series (right) uses many monthly points. It compares the data after the change with the trend expected from before (level and slope).

Ask: 'What else changed in your hospital in the month you started your last new protocol?' Expected: usually something.

Timing: 5 minutes.
:::

## Qualitative designs: when numbers cannot answer

::: {.neu-intro}
Why? How? What is it like? Words, not numbers, analysed as themes. One study can use one method, or combine them.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[In-depth interviews]{.neu-card-title}

- One person, open questions
- Usually 30-60 minutes
- e.g. why urine output goes unrecorded at night
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Focus groups]{.neu-card-title}

- 6-8 people discuss together
- Views spark other views
- e.g. how families experience consent in the ICU
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Observation]{.neu-card-title}

- Watch what people actually do
- It may differ from what they say
- e.g. how fluid charts are filled in
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Qualitative research explains why and how. It complements numbers.
:::

::: {.notes}
A study can use one method or all three. Combining them (triangulation) gives a fuller picture.

Sampling is purposive, until no new themes appear. Reporting: COREQ or SRQR.

Ask: 'One fluid question only interviews could answer?' Expected: why fluid charts are incomplete, why doctors hesitate to stop maintenance fluids.

Timing: 4.5 minutes.
:::

## Wrap-up: match the design to the question

| If your question is... | Start with | Example on our fluid question |
|:---|:---|:---|
| How common is it right now? | Cross-sectional | Positive fluid balance in our ICU today |
| Rare outcome: what raised the risk? | Case-control | New dialysis, looking back at the fluid received |
| What happens after an exposure? | Cohort | Positive balance and death by day 28 (Paper 2) |
| Does this treatment work? | RCT | Restrictive vs usual fluids (Paper 1) |
| Is the new option not worse? | Non-inferiority RCT | Cheaper restrictive strategy, mortality not worse |
| Is the change made for a whole unit? | Cluster RCT | Nurse-led fluid charting, randomise ICUs |
| A change already made on one date? | Interrupted time series | Monthly mortality before and after a bundle |
| Why? How? What is it like? | Qualitative | Why urine output goes unrecorded at night |
| Can we run the big trial? | Pilot study | Recruitment and delivery in our two ICUs |

::: {.neu-table-caption}
Start from the question, and the design follows from it. Then check that it is feasible in your setting.
:::

::: {.notes}
This table sums up 3.1 and 3.2 before the exercise. The next exercise uses it.

In the proposal builder everyone justifies their design this way: 'my question is about X, so the best feasible design is Y'. A retrospective cohort with honest limits is acceptable.

Poll: 'How many ICU patients have a positive fluid balance today?' Expected: cross-sectional.

Timing: 5.5 minutes. 3.2 ends here.
:::

## Exercise: choose the design

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#0D7377"}
WHOLE-CLASS TASK · 15 min
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#0D7377"}
- Five planning questions about our fluid question (exercise sheet, Part B)
- Then your own question: which design, and may you say 'caused' or only 'associated with'?
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
Use the table

- Start from the question
- Pick the design from the previous slide
- Then ask: is it feasible here?
:::
:::
::::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#0D7377"}
**OUTPUT** Work alone (5 min): a design, one reason and its main weakness for each question, then your own
:::

::: {.notes}
5 minutes: everyone works alone. Then about 1.5 minutes per question: call on two or three people for the design, a reason and the main weakness, and type them on screen. Last 3 minutes: two or three people say their own design and claim.

Answers: 1 non-inferiority RCT. 2 cluster RCT. 3 interrupted time series. 4 qualitative interviews or focus groups. 5 pilot or feasibility study.

Watch for: an RCT for a harm or prognosis question. Ask: could you ethically assign this?

Key: s3\_solutions, Part B.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Inclusion describes your P (Population). Exclusion removes eligible people for a stated reason.
:::

::: {.notes}
Proposal builder 3 starts here (3 minutes on this slide, then 42 minutes).

Boulet included ages 18-85 within 24 h of vasopressors, and excluded dialysis within 24 h, end-stage kidney disease and BMI below 18.

'Age under 18' is not an exclusion, it is simply not included.

Ask: 'One good exclusion for our fluid study?' Expected: chronic dialysis, comfort care only.

Timing: 3 minutes.
:::

## Proposal builder 3: design, setting and population

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#055F56"}
PROPOSAL BUILDER · 45 min
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#055F56"}
- Proposal Part 2, sections 2.1 to 2.3: design and justification, setting, population
- First the instructor writes them for the running example (15 min)
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#055F56"}
Check your draft

- Design matches the question?
- Feasible in your unit?
- Inclusion = your P (Population)?
- Each exclusion has a reason?
- 'Caused' or 'associated'?
:::
:::
::::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#055F56"}
**OUTPUT** Work alone (20 min): draft sections 2.1 to 2.3 for your own question (anything left: at home)
:::

::: {.notes}
15 minutes: fill in sections 2.1 to 2.3 of the template for the running example on screen, thinking aloud. 20 minutes: everyone drafts alone. 7 minutes: three volunteers read their design and justification for feedback.

Model: retrospective cohort, one adult ICU, 3 years. An RCT is not feasible without funding, so we say 'associated with'. Full model in s3\_solutions, Part C.

Watch for: an RCT for an exposure that cannot be assigned, a setting far too large, exclusions that repeat the inclusions.

Sections 2.4 and 2.5 could also be drafted now, but they are left for Session 4 to balance the two sessions.

Warn at 10 and 2 minutes before the end.
:::

## Session 3 in one slide

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[3.1 Basic designs]{.neu-card-title}

- Snapshot, look back, follow forward
- RCT: chance assigns the exposure
- RCT may say 'caused', cohort says 'associated'
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}

[Your proposal]{.neu-card-title}

- Design and justification
- Setting
- Inclusion and exclusion criteria
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** The question picks the design. The design decides what you may claim.

Ask three volunteers to explain one card each. If time is short, read the key message only.

Timing: 2 minutes.

DISCUSSION · 5 min
:::

::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#1F5C7A"}
- Exit question (in the chat): doctors chose restrictive fluids for some patients with septic shock and not for others, and both groups were followed to day 28. Which design? 'Caused' or 'associated'?
- Homework: finish sections 2.1 to 2.3 of your proposal
- Reading: 'Patients' in Paper 1 (Boulet) and 'Data source' in Paper 2 (Hyun)

Exit answer: a cohort. It may only say 'associated' (confounding by indication, next Saturday).

Next Saturday (Session 4): can we trust the result, and how big is the effect? Open Session 4 with three anonymous exit answers.

Timing: 3 minutes. Finish at 22:30.

## The decision tree in action: Paper 1 (Boulet) and Paper 2 (Hyun)

:::: {.neu-steps}
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Assigned?]{.neu-step-label}

- Boulet: yes, the trial assigned the strategy
- Hyun: no, clinicians decided
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Random?]{.neu-step-label}

- Boulet: yes, by a central computer
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Comparison?]{.neu-step-label}

- Hyun: yes, positive vs negative balance
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Time order?]{.neu-step-label}

- Hyun: exposure on days 1-3, then death by day 28
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#055F56"}
[Design]{.neu-step-label}

- Boulet: RCT
- Hyun: cohort
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Walk every paper through the same questions before reading its results.
:::

::: {.notes}
Use if 'Name that design' showed confusion. Then ask people to try a paper from their own reference list.

Timing: 2 minutes if used.
:::

## More practice (other examples): name the design

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#6C3483"}
QUICK QUIZ · 3 min
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#6C3483"}
- A. All 300 inpatients are checked today for a urinary catheter and for urinary infection
- B. Patients with ventilator-associated pneumonia are compared with patients without it for earlier sedation use
- C. Patients who received early mobilisation (the physiotherapist's decision) and those who did not are followed to discharge
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#6C3483"}
Choose

- Cross-sectional
- Case-control
- Cohort
- RCT
:::
:::
::::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#6C3483"}
**OUTPUT** One design named for each scenario (answers on the next slide)
:::

::: {.notes}
Watch for scenario C: two groups, but the physiotherapist decided, not chance.

Timing: 3 minutes with the answers, if used.
:::

## Answers: name the design (other examples)

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[A. Cross-sectional]{.neu-card-title}

- One day, everyone
- Exposure and outcome measured together
- Gives prevalence
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[B. Case-control]{.neu-card-title}

- Chosen by outcome (pneumonia)
- Look back for exposure (sedation)
- Gives an odds ratio
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[C. Cohort]{.neu-card-title}

- Grouped by exposure (mobilisation)
- Followed forward to discharge
- Not an RCT: nobody randomised
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Ask: chosen by exposure or by outcome? Assigned by chance or not?
:::

::: {.notes}
Two groups do not make a trial. Selected by outcome = case-control, by exposure = cohort.
:::

## More practice (other examples): which design?

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#6C3483"}
QUICK QUIZ · 3 min
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#6C3483"}
- A. A cheaper antibiotic schedule. We only need to show it is not worse
- B. A hand-hygiene programme delivered to whole wards
- C. Why do families refuse research consent in the ICU?
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#6C3483"}
Choose

- Cluster trial
- Non-inferiority trial
- Qualitative interviews
:::
:::
::::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#6C3483"}
**OUTPUT** One design for each (answers in the notes)
:::

::: {.notes}
Answers: A non-inferiority trial with a margin set in advance. B cluster RCT. C qualitative interviews or focus groups.

Timing: 3 minutes if used.
:::

## Choosing good controls in a case-control study

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Same source]{.neu-card-title}

- Same hospital, units and period as the cases
- Would have become a case if they had the outcome
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Same measurement]{.neu-card-title}

- Same records, same questions
- Ideally an assessor who does not know who is a case
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Matching (optional)]{.neu-card-title}

- e.g. age, month of admission
- Do not match on the exposure itself
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Bad controls make any case-control study meaningless.
:::

::: {.notes}
Controls from the same units and months. Measure exposure the same way in both groups. Do not over-match.

Timing: 2 minutes if used.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** The question (better, same, not worse) is fixed in the protocol, before the data.
:::

::: {.notes}
CI: confidence interval. Margin: the largest difference we accept, fixed in advance. Hypothetical results.

The bars are the 95% CIs of three example trials. The grey zone lies between the two margins, set before the trial. It is not a CI. Each row states where the whole CI must lie for that claim.

A failed superiority trial does not show equivalence: it had no margin.

Timing: 2 minutes if used.
:::

## Making an interrupted time series stronger

::: {.neu-intro}
e.g. when evaluating a quality-improvement project, such as a new sepsis bundle
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[More time points]{.neu-card-title}

- At least 8-12 points before and after
- Same definition every month
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[A control series]{.neu-card-title}

- A unit or hospital without the change
- Same months, same measure
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#B23B2E"}
[Record co-interventions]{.neu-card-title}

- Staff changes, new policies, audits
- Write them down as they happen
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** A before-after average is weak. A long, controlled time series is much stronger.
:::

::: {.notes}
Builds on the quasi-experimental slide of 3.2. More data points, a control series and a diary of other changes. Reporting: SQUIRE 2.0.

Timing: 2 minutes if used.
:::
